slides.title: 1 Had better They’d better extend the laurel leaf or this will take longer. Statements can go in negative form or questions too. 2 Can + verb I truly think we can get back on the horse right away. 3 Should + Verb We should sit them in semi-circle so they see each others’ faces. Thanks, Mark for hitting the ball rolling. To Consider 1. Had better or ‘d better is used to mean = It would be a good idea if / It would be better if… 2. People tend to confuse had better with would better which does not exist as a grammatical construction. 3. Used in the right contexts, should and can can also state an idea to be helpful.

Statements can go in negative form or questions too. 2 Can + verb I truly think we can get back on the horse right away. 3 Should + Verb We should sit them in semi-circle so they see each others’ faces. Thanks, Mark for hitting the ball rolling. To Consider 1. Had better or ‘d better is used to mean = It would be a good idea if / It would be better if… 2. People tend to confuse had better with would better which does not exist as a grammatical construction. 3. Used in the right contexts, should and can can also state an idea to be helpful.
There are many ways in which we can express ideas or suggestions when we want to be helpful.

slides.title: Let’s take a look how we may express ideas or suggestions.
visibleTexts: Let’s take a look how we may express ideas or suggestions.

Functions Examples 1 State a more appealing option They’d better not take those samples until they are ready. 2 Come up with ideas Children can share the magazines in small teams to finish faster, don’t you think? 3 Reflect on a thought Shouldn’t we look into it before making a choice? To consider 1. The use of had better, can and should is not fixed to the functions of the examples. 2. Given the context, each of them can work with any of the functions. 3. Should can be used as an alternative to if. E.G: Should you need internet, the code is in this card.

slides.title: Successful Managers Know That Luck Goes With Effort Experienced managers learn that success is a combination of luck and effort. Arrogant and inexperienced managers may think any success is entirely from effort. They’d better change that idea. Anyone who works in management long enough will see many managers rise and fall according to their measures of luck and effort. Some of the managers who fall end up rising again through ambition and perseverance while others do not. Firings, demotions, layoffs and personal problems derail many careers. The ones who bounce back, lick their wounds and find a way to rise once more so they can superpass whatever makes them fall. The most successful managers have exceptional traits including higher than average intelligence, character, ambition, energy and leadership skills. But luck does play a part. Even they can’t control everything or guarantee success in any and all situations; shouldn’t this be something to think of? For example, a senior manager who took over a struggling operation couldn’t do anything about a key subordinate who sadly was dying of leukemia. Nor could he do anything about other underperforming business units that were dragging down the entire division, which ultimately led to its demise. Article retrieved and adapted from: https://medium.com/leading-and-managing/successful-managers-know-that-luck-goes-with-effort-d4cf6bc439a2
